architecture: StackVitals has no hosted backend. Everything happens in three places you already have: a GitHub Actions job in your repo, a branch of your repo, and the reader's browser. The diagram shows one run from start to finish; the sections under it walk through it panel by panel. ## Reading the diagram Blue arrows are data moving through a run. Dashed blue lines are optional or public data. The dashed grey line is the way back: settings and decisions made in the app. ### 1. What starts a run A run starts when any of these happens: a CI run finishes (`workflow_run`), the 3-hour schedule comes round, a deploy or incident is sent from another tool (`stackvitals record`), someone makes a request in the app (`workflow_dispatch`), someone comments `/stackvitals` on an issue or pull request, or the workflow or settings file changes (`push`). Each start is the same job; what it reads depends on what started it. ### 2. Collect The job reads from GitHub with the repo's own token: Actions runs and their logs, test reports (JUnit and the other formats in [quickstart.md](quickstart.md#what-next)), pull requests and reviews, issues and comments, deployments and releases, and the lockfiles and workflows in the repo. It reads only what is new since the last run. When the API budget runs low it saves what it has, and the next run carries on. Connectors are optional and use keys you add as repository secrets: Jira, Linear, PagerDuty, incident.io, SonarQube, Copilot usage, Slack, Teams and Discord ([connectors.md](connectors.md)). ### 3. Analyse Six modules read the same collected data in one pass: CI Health (flaky tests and the verdict on each failing pull request), Team Flow (who has to act next), Delivery and DORA (deploys, lead time and failures), Dependencies (vulnerable and risky packages), Community (newcomers and first answers) and Portal (owners and scorecards). Insights then puts every module's findings in one list, ranked by the hours at stake. Every verdict stands on two things: the **rules registry**, where each rule has an accuracy card measured on public repos with its losses ([rules.md](rules.md), [accuracy.md](accuracy.md)), and the **peer benchmarks**, updated daily, that say how similar repos compare. ### 4. Save The job opens one shallow checkout of the `stackvitals-data` branch, writes what every module found and makes one commit. If another run pushed first, every step runs again on the fresh data, so overlapping runs never lose each other's work. Housekeeping keeps each stream for its retention period and holds the branch under a size cap (250 MB by default), dropping the oldest days first. ### 5. Data branch `stackvitals-data` is a branch of your own repo, so it has the repo's access rules: on a private repo, only people who can read the repo can read it. It holds plain files, no database: | Folder | What it holds | |---|---| | `ci/` `flow/` `deps/` `community/` `portal/` `connectors/` | the history, one gzipped file per day per stream | | `summary/` | the tables the app, Explore and agents read | | `decisions/log.ndjson` | every decision and settings change: who made it and why | | `docs/` | the web app's files, which GitHub Pages serves | ### 6. What you get - **Web app**: on your GitHub Pages for a public repo, or on your machine with `stackvitals ui owner/repo` for a private one. It is static files that read `summary/`; Explore runs SQL in your browser. - **PR comment and verdict check**: one comment sorts each CI failure as likely flaky, already failing on main, or new. - **Issues and alerts**: issues for flaky tests, and messages to Slack, Teams or Discord. These are sent only after the save, so a re-run never posts twice. - **MCP server**: AI agents ask the same data (`stackvitals serve`). - **CLI**: reports, setup, SQL and exports from a terminal (`pip install stackvitals`). Settings and decisions made in the app come back as issues (or, with your own token, as commits); the next run applies them and records them in `decisions/log.ndjson`. ### Project side What one repo can't know on its own, like how similar repos compare, comes from the project's own crawler: scheduled workflows that sample about 125,000 public repos and publish only aggregates, never any repo's data, to the public `bench-latest` release. Your job downloads those numbers; it never sends your data back. ## More detail ### One job, one commit Each run of the Action opens one shallow checkout of the `stackvitals-data` branch, runs every module named in `modules:` against it, keeps house (retention, the size cap) and commits once ([core/workspace.py](../src/stackvitals/core/workspace.py)). If another run pushed first, the push is rejected and every step runs again on the fresh data, so overlapping runs converge without losing either side. What talks to people (comments, issues, chat) runs only after the commit, so a refused comment never loses data and a re-run never posts twice. A module that fails is reported in the job summary; the others still run and save. A run that runs out of API budget saves what it read and says what it left; the next run carries on. ### Storage History is plain files: one gzipped NDJSON file per day per stream, with retention per stream (CI days 180 days, transitions and closed pull requests 400, Copilot 730) and a size cap (250 MB by default) that drops the oldest days first ([scaling.md](scaling.md)). Busy public repos store about 1 KB per CI run. An opt-in squash rewrites the branch's git history to one commit every 1,000 commits; the files stay byte for byte. Nothing in the branch is a secret: tokens and keys live in Actions secrets, and on a public repo, tracker titles, links and people's affiliations are never written ([privacy.md](privacy.md)). ### The app The app is static: Preact and TypeScript bundled ahead of time (`web/`, built into the package) and copied into the branch's `docs/` folder as `index.html` and `app/`, with a content security policy that allows only its own scripts. Explore and the printable module pages are separate pages that load DuckDB and Chart.js from public CDNs at pinned versions. It reads the JSON tables the job wrote. Settings and decisions made in the app are sent as GitHub issues or comments that the next job applies, or, with the person's own GitHub token, committed or run straight from the browser; either way GitHub checks the sender's permissions and the change is recorded in `decisions/log.ndjson`. Explore loads DuckDB in the browser (from jsDelivr) to run SQL over the same tables. ### Rules and their evidence The verdicts and headline numbers come from rules listed in [bench/accuracy/registry.json](../bench/accuracy/registry.json): what it was tuned on, the held-out data it was checked on, the bar it had to meet and every change since ([rules.md](rules.md)). Each card in `bench/accuracy/` holds the method and the results; [accuracy.md](accuracy.md) is generated from them, and a test fails when a page and its data disagree. ### Cross-repo evidence What a single repo can't know (how similar repos compare, whether an upgrade broke other projects, how a maintainer reviews outsiders) comes from a crawl of public repos (a list of about 125,000, about 90,000 of them sampled for CI benchmarks) run by the project's own scheduled workflows in `deploy/crawler/`. It publishes aggregates only. Your job reads them; it never sends your data back. ### Code map | Folder | What it holds | |---|---| | `src/stackvitals/ci` | CI Health: collecting runs and test reports, flake detection, the PR verdict, automation | | `src/stackvitals/flow` | Team Flow: who acts next, review stages, preflight | | `src/stackvitals/core` | the shared job (workspace, store, settings, decisions), Delivery and DORA, Insights, Explore, the app's data | | `src/stackvitals/deps` | Dependency Steward | | `src/stackvitals/community` | Community health | | `src/stackvitals/portal` | Portal: catalog, owners, scorecards, campaigns, golden paths, the org view | | `src/stackvitals/connectors` | Jira, Linear, PagerDuty, incident.io, Copilot, Slack, Discord, Discourse | | `src/stackvitals/web` | the app and the site | | `src/stackvitals/mcp_server.py` | the MCP server | | `src/mergescout` | Contribute (MergeScout) | | `bench/accuracy` | accuracy cards, the rule registry and the generators for the accuracy pages | | `worker/` | optional Cloudflare Worker for instant alerts | | `deploy/crawler` | the crawler's workflows |
roadmap:
What comes next, in rough order. Dates are when the data allows a result, not promises. Suggestions are welcome as
issues; the ones backed by a real repo's problem move up.

## Checks already running, read on a date

- **Does the issue finder pick issues outsiders get merged?** Its ranking was frozen and its picks recorded before the
  outcomes existed. Read from 2027-03-20, when the attempt and merge windows have closed
  ([bench/accuracy/contribute](../bench/accuracy/contribute/README.md)).
- **Do agents answer older CI failures better with StackVitals?** On failures inside GitHub's 90-day log retention it
  added nothing measurable. The test that matters is on failures whose logs GitHub has deleted; it runs once enough of
  the recorded failures have passed GitHub's 90-day retention ([bench/accuracy/agents](../bench/accuracy/agents/README.md)).

## Accuracy

- A person's audit of a sample of every card's labels; today two model families label and no person has checked.
- Status precision for flaky CI: re-running pinned commits to confirm flakes directly, not only from history.
- Deployment detection for shipping workflows with plain names (docker, pypi, CD), the weak side of today's rule.

## Coverage

- Bors and other merge bots outside GitHub's merge queue; monorepo task runners (Nx, Turborepo, Bazel) that skip
  unchanged tests; GitHub Enterprise Server. Each is untested today ([limitations.md](limitations.md#failure-modes)).
- Dependency dossiers beyond npm and PyPI, and dependency paths from poetry and pip lockfiles.
- GitLab merge requests, deployments and incidents (CI already runs inside GitLab).

## Not planned

- A hosted service or an account: the suite stays in your repo.
- Productivity scores for individuals. Where StackVitals names people (an owner, who acts next on a pull request), it
  is to route work, not to rate them.
settings:
Put these in `.github/stackvitals.toml` on your default branch. A merged change applies on the next run (the workflow
runs when the file is pushed). A missing file means the defaults; a value StackVitals can't use keeps its
default and is named in the job summary. The app's Settings page edits the same file.

| `min_events` | `2` | Fail-then-pass events with no code change before a test or job is flaky. |
| `quiet_days` | `14` days | Days without a flake before the pass-on-retry monitor lets go. |
| `quiet_runs` | `10` runs | Clean runs in a row before a flaky test counts as fixed. |

## [ci.monitors.failure_rate]

| Key | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|

| `window_runs` | `50` runs | Latest default-branch runs the failure rate looks at. |
| `min_runs` | `20` runs | Runs needed before the failure-rate monitor can fire. |
| `activate` | `0.15` | Failure share that turns the monitor on. |
| `resolve` | `0.05` | The monitor stays on while the failure share is above this. |

| `key_expires` | `""` | When the Discord bot token expires, if it does; a warning shows 14 days before. |

## [connectors.pagerduty]

| Key | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `services` | `[] (none)` | PagerDuty service ids whose incidents count; empty counts every service the key can see. |
| `urgencies` | `["high"]` | Which PagerDuty urgencies count as production incidents. |
| `key_expires` | `""` | When the PagerDuty key expires, if it does; a warning shows 14 days before. |

## [connectors.incident_io]

| Key | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `incident_types` | `[] (none)` | incident.io incident types that count, like Platform; empty counts every type (test and tutorial incidents never count). |
| `key_expires` | `""` | When the incident.io key expires, if it does; a warning shows 14 days before. |

## [connectors.copilot]

| Key | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `org` | `""` | The organization whose Copilot usage reports to keep; empty means this repo's owner. |
| `key_expires` | `""` | When the Copilot reports token expires, if it does; a warning shows 14 days before. |

## [connectors.sonar]

| Key | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `url` | `"https://sonarcloud.io"` | SonarCloud (https://sonarcloud.io) or your SonarQube server. |
| `project` | `""` | The Sonar project key, like myorg_myrepo; its quality gate and measures are read each day. A private project or SonarQube server needs the SONAR_TOKEN secret. |
| `key_expires` | `""` | When the Sonar token expires, if one is used; a warning shows 14 days before. |

## [connectors.ai_spend]

| Key | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `key_expires` | `""` | When the soonest of the AI spend admin keys (Anthropic, OpenAI, Cursor) expires, if it does; a warning shows 14 days before. |

Example:

```toml
[alerts]
pickup_p75_hours = 6
channels = ["webhook", "issue"]

[ci.mute]
"tests/test_api.py::test_slow_network" = 2026-12-31

[automation]
issues = true
```
